primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: After birth, effective pulmonary oxygenation abruptly raises tissue oxygen availability. This reduces hypoxia-driven erythropoietin production and transiently suppresses erythropoiesis, contributing to the normal postnatal fall in hemoglobin concentration in healthy term infants.
vignette: A healthy 10-week-old term infant is seen for routine care. Growth and feeding are normal, and there is no jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly. Compared with the newborn period, the hemoglobin concentration has fallen and the anemia is normocytic and normochromic with a low reticulocyte count. Ferritin is adequate and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.
lead: Which physiologic change most directly accounts for this infant's decreased erythrocyte production?
correct: Increased tissue oxygenation after birth suppresses erythropoietin production
distractors: Depletion of iron stores causes iron-restricted erythropoiesis
Maternal IgG antibodies accelerate immune destruction of the infant's erythrocytes
Parvovirus B19 infection destroys erythroid precursor cells
Reduced beta-globin synthesis causes ineffective erythropoiesis
distractor_notes: Iron deficiency causes iron-restricted, typically microcytic anemia and is inconsistent with adequate ferritin and the expected normocytic physiologic nadir in this healthy term infant.
Hemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn is caused by maternal IgG against fetal RBC antigens and is associated with hemolysis; the infant has no jaundice and a negative direct antiglobulin test.

Parvovirus B19 replicates in erythroid precursor cells and can cause reticulocytopenia/red-cell aplasia, but it is a pathologic infection rather than the normal postnatal decline occurring in a well infant.
Beta-thalassemia reduces beta-globin synthesis and produces a microcytic hemoglobinopathy; it does not explain the normal, transient normocytic postnatal anemia driven by reduced erythropoietin.
key_expl: Healthy term infants normally develop a transient postnatal decline in hemoglobin. At birth, lung expansion and effective oxygenation markedly increase tissue oxygen delivery. Because erythropoietin production is stimulated by tissue hypoxia, improved oxygenation suppresses erythropoietin and erythropoiesis until the falling hemoglobin again increases the erythropoietic drive.
objective: Explain physiologic anemia of infancy as a normal postnatal adaptation in which improved tissue oxygenation suppresses erythropoietin and transiently reduces erythrocyte production.
clues: healthy term infant around the physiologic nadir

sources.title: Perinatal Anemia
sources.locator: Etiology of Perinatal Anemia — Physiologic anemia
sources.support: Merck states that in term infants increased oxygenation with breathing after birth raises tissue oxygen, negatively feeds back on erythropoietin production and erythropoiesis, and contributes to a physiologic normocytic-normochromic hemoglobin decline during the first 2 to 3 months.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Anemia
sources.support: NCBI states that renal erythropoietin is the principal hormonal regulator of erythropoiesis and that tissue hypoxia is its primary physiologic stimulus through hypoxia-inducible signaling.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Infant Nutrition Requirements and Options
sources.support: NCBI states that iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia and notes that iron requirements and depletion patterns differ from the normal early physiologic anemia of a healthy term infant.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Hemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn
sources.support: NCBI states that HDFN is caused by maternal IgG-mediated destruction of fetal/neonatal RBCs and that a direct antiglobulin test identifies antibody-coated infant RBCs in immune hemolytic disease.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine, NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Parvoviruses
sources.support: NCBI states that parvovirus B19 replicates in committed erythroid precursor cells and can produce erythroid aplasia with reticulocytopenia.

sources.title: Beta Thalassemia
sources.support: NCBI describes beta-thalassemia as reduced or absent beta-globin synthesis producing a microcytic hemoglobinopathy rather than the normal postnatal EPO-suppression pattern.
